lines.note: The opening do completes puxando on f195. Uma wo hikiyosuru means drawing the horse closer, matching chegar o caualo.
Hikizan is subtraction. Diminuir nas contas confirms the arithmetic sense and the damaged initial F; Gisan is a cross-reference, not a continuation.
Hikizuri means dragging along. The printed conjugational ending utta is retained, also recorded by NINJAL, rather than regularized from modern hikizutta.
Hikwa raku-yō evokes falling blossoms and leaves. The scan shows a circumflex in racuyô; roſas is the dictionary's floral gloss, not necessarily a modern botanical restriction.
Lhas completes folhas: the leaves fall together with the flowers. S marks written usage of the preceding expression.
Hikwan here denotes a servant or retainer, directly glossed criado. It is separate from the following two emotional terms.
The visibly separated Fi quan pairs sorrow and joy: canaximi and yorocobi. Treating it as the preceding retainer word would obscure the bilingual contrast.
Alegria completes the paired definition, sorrow and joy. The final S is a usage label rather than Japanese text.
Te no hira is the palm of the hand. The example establishes the broad flat-surface sense shared with the following sword example.
Katana no hira denotes the flat of a sword blade. Eſpada restores the missing letter in the OCR's e pada; the gloss is not about a separate object.
Hirauchi ni suru and katana no hira de utsu are alternatives for striking with the blade's flat. The final v belongs to divided vtçu.
Tçu completes utsu. Dar deſpaldeiradas describes blows with a sword's flat and confirms the preceding Japanese construction.

runs.text: O estender, ou alargar a caſa como

lines.note: Hirabari refers here to extending a house or its enclosure, not the lancet sense below. The following line supplies the means of extension.

runs.text: fazendo algũa ſebe, ou eſtendendo cortinas.

lines.note: The explanation specifies a hedge or stretched curtains. Preserve the printed nasal abbreviation in algũa rather than expanding it.
Hirabari wo utsu is the construction illustrated. The damaged abbreviation is Vt, introducing an example, not a pilcrow followed by t.

runs.text: ou estender a caſa deſta maneira. ¶ Item,

lines.note: The gloss completes enlarging the house in this manner. Item then introduces the homonymous implement below.
Hirabari now means a lancet for bloodletting, used on horses or people. This is a distinct lexical sense under the repeated form.
Homẽs, people, completes the object list. Hirabari wo tatsuru means applying the lancet; lã begins the divided Portuguese lancet-stroke word.
Çetada completes lãçetada: a puncture made to draw blood. The nasal abbreviation and physical line break are retained.
Hirabira to shitaru mono describes a spread-out, broad thing. Both scan and the repeated example resolve the damaged initial headword as Firabira.
No completes mono. The Portuguese describes something broad and extended; the compressed Couſalarga is left as printed.

runs.text: Certa feição de portal, ou fron-

lines.note: Hirakado is a form of gateway or frontage. Its damaged middle letters are supported by the gate gloss and the NINJAL entry.
Teſpicio completes fronteſpicio, the building frontage. This is a continuation, not another Japanese headword.
Hirachi is equated with heiji, level ground. Terra praina preserves the historical Portuguese form rather than modern plana.

runs.text: Aparte larga do peſcoço do caualo.

lines.note: Hirakubi denotes the broad part of a horse's neck. The animal qualification distinguishes it from an unrestricted anatomical term.
Hirakuchi is a viper. The regional label Cami introduces the alternative kuchihami, divided across the next line.
Chifami completes Cu-chifami, kuchihami. It is the regional snake name, not an independent entry beginning chi.

runs.text: Certo grao de dignidade dos Cũgues

lines.note: Hirakuge denotes a rank among ordinary court nobles. The Portuguese-adapted Cũgues refers to kuge and remains distinct from the Japanese headword.
Ordinarios qualifies the nobles in the preceding definition, completing that rank description.
Hirada or hirata is a broad, low boat. Latin l introduces the alternative pronunciation rather than a Japanese consonant.

runs.text: xa como ſe vſa nos rios.

lines.note: Xa completes baixa; the example is the kind of low vessel used on rivers. No additional word is supplied at the unmarked break.

runs.text: Caldeirão, ou panella de ferro lar-

lines.note: Hiragama is a broad iron kettle or pot. The scan and the vessel gloss support gama rather than the OCR's gania.

runs.text: ga, & baixa com hũa cinta ao redor.

lines.note: Ga completes larga, then baixa and the encircling band further describe the pot. The OCR's Sà was a misread continuation, not an accented word.

runs.text: Certa laya de letras de Iapão.

lines.note: Hiragana names a kind of Japanese writing. The familiar lexical identity is corroborated by the scan, which restores the damaged F and n.

runs.text: Certas aranhas que tem o corpo, ou

lines.note: Hiragumo denotes flat-bodied spiders. The gloss starts with their body and continues with the back in the next line.

runs.text: coſtas largas q̃ estão metidas nalgum bolſo, ou

lines.note: Costas largas describes broad backs; the spiders occupy a pouch-like web. Costas and estão restore meaningful letters lost by OCR.

runs.text: tea que tem feito em algum canto, &c.

lines.note: The web is made in a corner or similar place. This completes the spider description rather than defining tea as a Japanese word.
Hiraguke no obi is a broad sash sewn like a tube or sheath. The damaged initial F is recoverable from the scan and headword reference.
Bainha supplies the sheath-like construction of the sash. It completes como rather than beginning another item.
Hirai means broad and thin. The two indented forms below are its nominal and adverbial derivatives, not unrelated headwords.
Firasa is the nominal derivative, breadth or flatness, of hirai. Its indentation links it to the preceding adjective.
Firǒ is the contracted adverbial form associated with hirai. Preserve the printed caron without converting the Level 1 text to a modern spelling.

runs.text: Fortaleza que eſta em terra praina.

lines.note: Hirajō is a fortress on level ground, a flatland castle. The Portuguese definition makes the damaged j legible as part of jō rather than iō.
Hiramekasu means making something flash or shimmer by movement. It is transitive, unlike hirameku at the next column's opening.
The examples are moving weapons or a katana. Catana is embedded in Portuguese explanatory syntax and is eligible for a typeface toggle.
Ōgi wo hiramekasu means waving a fan. The damaged spelling Vǒguuo is retained as seen, rather than silently normalizing it to the clearer Vǒguiuo elsewhere on the page.
Rar completes virar: moving and turning the fan. The line belongs to the example above, not a footer.
Hirameku is fluttering, exemplified by flags. Bandei continues into bandeiras on the next line.

runs.text: ras, bulir papel, &c. com o vento. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Paper moves in the wind; bulir supplies the coherent Portuguese verb where OCR read bualir. Item introduces the shining-weapon sense.

runs.text: Reluzir a eſpada, ou armas que ſe mouem, ou

lines.note: A sword or other moving weapon gleams. This continues hirameku, not the preceding transitive hiramekasu entry.
Meneão completes the movement clause: weapons that are moved or waved. It is Portuguese verbal text, not a separate label.
Hiramu means shrinking or wilting. The following fear context gives the figurative sense of recoiling or losing courage.

runs.text: cõ medo, &c. ¶ Item, No Ximo chorar:

lines.note: Fear motivates the shrinking; in Ximo the word can also refer to crying. The regional limitation matters to the second sense.
Naqi firamu, naki-hiramu, is offered as the preferable expression for the crying sense. Meliùs is editorial Latin and remains italic.
Hirani is an adverb meaning humbly or emphatically in any case. Humildemente, not Hamildemente, is supported by the printed vowel and the examples.
Hirani tanomu is an earnest request. Encare continues into encarecidamente and translates the force of the adverb.
Hirani fusu means prostrating oneself. Proſtrarſe restores the damaged r in the Portuguese verb, consistent with de bruços below.
De bruços specifies lying face down. It completes the prostration gloss, not a further Japanese expression.
Hirakeru is to open, as a door opens. The inflectional listing is followed by a cosmological example.
Ame tsuchi hirake hajimatte yori means since heaven and earth began to open or separate. The doubled t in fajimatte is supported by the scan and Japanese morphology.

runs.text: Depois de ſe ſeparar, & aparecer. i, Deſe

lines.note: The gloss says after separation and appearance; i introduces an explanatory restatement. Deſe is retained across the physical break before formar.

runs.text: formar o ceo, & a terra. ¶ Item, Abri

lines.note: The restatement is the formation of heaven and earth. Item then shifts to flowers opening, with Abri continued below.

runs.text: remſe as roſas, ou flores. Vt,

lines.note: Flowers open; hana ga begins the Japanese example. The fi at the edge belongs to firaquru, not an independent word.
Firaquru completes hirakuru, but the dictionary explicitly prefers the alternative construction on the next line. That usage distinction should not be normalized away.
Naga completes Fa-naga, hana ga hiraku. The preferred form is hiraku rather than the preceding hirakuru.
Hiraku means to open; mon wo hira-qu opens a gate. The repeated verb and visible letters correct both Abir and fita in the draft.
Qu completes hiraku. Manaco begins the next example, opening the eyes; its particle is carried onto the following line.
Manako wo hiraku means opening one's eyes. Fushin wo then introduces the figurative resolution of doubt.
Fushin wo hiraku is dispelling a doubt, matching soltar a duuida. The next hana ga example returns to a flower opening.
Raqu completes hiraku in the flower example. Hachi wo hiraku then introduces begging with an alms bowl.

runs.text: Pedir eſmola, propriamente ſe diz de Bonzos,

lines.note: The alms-begging use is specifically said of bonzes. Propriamente is an explanatory adverb, not part of the Japanese example.
Religiosos restates bonzes. Kyō wo han ni or hangi ni hiraku describes printing texts; the damaged Qiǒ is read in that Buddhist-book context, not as an isolated rǒ.
Ni firaqu completes the printing expression. Qiyet begins the checked-final-t expression for great joy, continued with no mayu below.
Kietsu no mayu wo hiraku evokes unknitting the brow in joy. Alegrarſe muito confirms the emotional meaning without expanding printed Qiyet.

Riun wo hiraku means obtaining victory or favorable fortune. The second enlarged scan pass resolves Riunuo, rather than the first-pass Riuuo; the Portuguese alcançar victoria supports the interpretation.
Ōgi wo hiraku is opening a fan. The caron is visible here, while the word's mechanics are independent of modern kana normalization.
Kura wo hiraku introduces opening a storehouse. The Portuguese identifies this as a non-Christian New Year custom.

runs.text: tas do gudão pollo anno nouo nalgum dia bom,

lines.note: The storehouse doors are opened on a good day at New Year. Bom, not hom, supplies the adjective required by dia and visible in the scan.
The good, cheerful day completes that custom. Dōgu wo hiraku then concerns displaying an implement for the first time.

runs.text: a primeira vez em publico algũa peça, &v-

lines.note: A piece is first brought out publicly. Primeira and publico repair OCR letter errors; the final v begins vſar below.
Vſar della completes using that piece. Chawanbiraki wo suru describes first use of a tea bowl; ſuru corrects the semantically impossible iuru.

runs.text: ſar a primeira vez dalgũa Chauan, & dar

lines.note: The gloss says using a bowl for the first time and showing it. The visible hauan is retained despite the expected chawan-derived form.
Della completes showing the bowl. A further hiraki sense begins, describing withdrawal in combat.

runs.text: colherſe no jugar das armas, ou retirarſe.

lines.note: In fencing, hiraku can mean contracting or drawing back. This contrasts with the ordinary opening sense above.
Shitsuke-gata no tsume hiraki concerns advancing and retreating in courteous conduct. Xitçuqe, not Mitçuqe, is supported by the scan and etiquette gloss.

runs.text: corteſias, agaſalhados, &c. o ſair com fer

lines.note: Courtesies and hospitality illustrate energetic approach. Fer continues into fervor below; no hyphen is supplied merely for lexical completion.
Withdrawal comes at its proper time. Mai and the divided dãgui introduce dance and discourse as the next applications.
Mai, dangui nado no tsume-hiraki describes measured advance and relaxation in dancing, preaching and other performances. The second pass resolves nadono, connecting the examples with “and the like”.

runs.text: uor no canto, bailo, prègaçaõ, &c, & reti-

lines.note: Singing, dancing and preaching exemplify the energetic phase. Reti continues into retirarſe and completes the contrasting withdrawal.
The performer withdraws or becomes quiet at the appropriate time. This closes the long series under hiraku.
Hirakiawaseru describes meeting or crossing in sword blows. The printed headword restores the damaged F without changing its inflectional endings.

runs.text: atanas nos golpes, ou talhos da eſgrima.

lines.note: The encounter is between katanas in fencing strokes. This specifies the martial sense rather than a generic meeting.
Hirakido is a hinged door. Couceira names the hinge-side support and is distinct from the OCR's couccira.
Hirakiwakareru means drawing apart or separating. The missing c is recoverable in the scan and supported by wakareru; diui continues physically below.
Printed catchword anticipating the opening of f197; verified against that scan. Preserved outside body text with its original stable ID.
